title: Parts Compatibility
seoTitle: Design a Parts Compatibility Feature for an E-commerce Site
description: Design "Does this fit my car?" — modelling vehicle fitment data, ingesting supplier catalogs, fast compatibility checks and filtered search by vehicle.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is a Parts Compatibility Feature?
blocks.text: Auto-parts and electronics stores let shoppers pick their vehicle (year, make, model, engine) or device and then show only parts that fit, with a "Fits your 2019 Honda Civic" badge on product pages.

items: Users should be able to select and save a vehicle (year → make → model → trim/engine).
Product pages should show whether a part fits the selected vehicle.
Search and category pages should filter to parts that fit the selected vehicle.
Catalog teams should be able to import fitment data from suppliers.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Compatibility checks on product pages in < 50ms.
Filtered search in < 300ms over tens of millions of parts.
Fitment data must be accurate — wrong answers cause returns and lost trust.
Catalog imports of millions of fitment rows shouldn't affect shopper traffic.
**Vehicle**: a normalised configuration (year, make, model, submodel, engine) with an ID — industry standards like ACES provide these.
**Part**: a product with SKU and attributes.
**Fitment**: a (partId, vehicleId) pair, optionally with qualifiers ("front axle only", "with sunroof").

blocks.code:
GET  /vehicles/makes?year=2019 ; /vehicles/models?year&make ; /vehicles?year&make&model -> Vehicle[]
GET  /parts/:sku/fitment?vehicleId=123 -> { fits: true, notes: "Front only" }
GET  /search?q=brake+pads&vehicleId=123 -> Part[]
POST /fitment/imports (catalog teams, file upload)

blocks.text: The vehicle catalog is small (hundreds of thousands of configurations) and changes rarely, so the cascading dropdown APIs are served from an in-memory cache or CDN. The chosen vehicle ID is stored in the user's garage (and a cookie for anonymous users).
The **Fitment Service** answers "does part X fit vehicle Y?" with a lookup on the fitment table keyed by `(partId, vehicleId)`, cached in Redis — e.g. a set of vehicle IDs per part.

Each part document in the search index carries the list of vehicle IDs it fits. A search with a selected vehicle adds a filter `vehicleIds: 123`, which search engines evaluate efficiently with an inverted index.
Supplier files are uploaded, validated and normalised against the vehicle catalog in a batch pipeline, written to the fitment database, and then pushed to the search index incrementally.
1) How do we model fitment compactly?

approach.text: Store "Fits 2016-2020 Civic" as text on the product.

challenges.text: Can't be filtered or verified, and spelling variations break matching.

approach.text: Explicit pairs keyed by normalised vehicle IDs — simple and precise.

challenges.text: A universal part can fit tens of thousands of vehicles, so the table reaches billions of rows.

blocks.title: Normalised pairs + range expansion at import

approach.text: Suppliers describe fitment as ranges ("2016-2020 Civic, all trims"). Store the compact rule, expand it into vehicle IDs at import time, and index the expanded IDs (compressed integer lists are cheap in search engines). Keep qualifiers as structured attributes so the UI can say "fits with conditions".

challenges.text: Expansion must re-run when the vehicle catalog adds new trims.

blocks.text: 2) How do we keep data accurate?

Validate imports against the vehicle catalog (reject unknown vehicles), diff each import against the previous version and flag large changes for review, track return reasons like "doesn't fit" to find bad fitment, and let catalog staff correct data with an audit trail.

quiz.question: Why normalise vehicles to IDs?
options: Free-text descriptions can't be reliably matched or filtered
quiz.explanation: IDs make fitment precise and filterable.

quiz.question: How does search filter to parts that fit a vehicle?
options: Index each part's list of vehicle IDs and filter on the selected ID
quiz.explanation: Inverted indexes make ID filters fast.

quiz.question: Why expand fitment ranges at import time?
options: So queries become simple ID lookups at read time
quiz.explanation: Expensive expansion moves offline; reads stay fast.

quiz.question: What signal helps find inaccurate fitment data?
quiz.explanation: Real-world returns point to bad data.
